translation:
_Rasik jan Jivan bhaye, kini bhakti prakash. Nahana nikat bolaayke, rakhya charan nivash. ||1||_ (Jivan[das] became a devoted seeker and made the light of bhakti [devotion] shine forth; calling Nahana near him, he gave him a home at his feet.)

_Gaam hamara Darapara, Sai hamara Ram. Sadguru Jivandasji, Parakh dhariya naam. ||2||_ (Our village is Darapara, our Lord [Sai] is Ram; our true guru is Jivandasji — I took on the name Parekh [as his disciple].)

The papers recording the time when Jivanji Maharaj departed to the eternal abode were burned in the original satsang (holy company/gathering). So Nana Parekh supplied the missing account, and in it he mentions his native place, Darapara. It was in this village that he began his own independent preaching. He had received initiation into Uda Dharma (the tradition's ascetic vow) from Dwarkadas, the grandson of Jivanji Maharaj. His tulsi-kyaros (tulsi-plant memorial platforms marking a departed saint's resting place) are at Darapura, ranging from Jivanji down to Nana Parekh. Thus this place is a sacred site.
